item.title: Rights groups urge sanctions after ICJ finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
item.description:
Fleeing violence and persecution, Rohingya refugees walk after crossing the Naf River from Myanmar into Bangladesh on Oct. 9, 2017. Photo by Fred Dufour/AFP via Getty Images In a 9-6 vote, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya people in the northern Rakhine State. This is a remarkable moment for the Rohingya people and international justice – the first time, in fact, that the ICJ has ever ruled that a state committed this crime. It is a historic victory, worthy of celebration in a world where good things happen all too sparsely. Especially because it is a victory won against a global legal architecture almost designed to never find that a state committed genocide. item.title: Brooks and Capehart on Trump's summit with Putin and Xi
item.description:
China's Xi Jinping places himself firmly in the center of the trilateral summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Doug Mills/Getty Images It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit , for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders. Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine , Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them. But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver? As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School , I saw a lot of style, but less substance. item.title: Removal of hat inside Fiona the hippo was 'impossible', Cincinnati Zoo says
item.description:
It was, it seems, a freak accident. Around two weeks ago, a child standing by Hippo Cove at the Cincinnati Zoo tossed a knit cap into the air, which was caught by a whirling ceiling fan and launched through the one-foot gap between the 12-foot-tall viewing window and the ceiling, where it landed in the enclosure's pool. Because Nile hippos can grow to be 3,000 pounds, zookeepers and veterinarians are not allowed to share space. There must be a protective barrier between the hippos and the humans, which prevented the swift removal of the hat. This is how Fiona the celebrity hippopotamus ate the hat that would kill her. After Fiona ate the hat, veterinarians started monitoring the hippo's progress in passing the object. They took her off exhibit. They offered her treats to encourage digestion. item.title: COP31 deal stalls as nations struggle to agree on climate plan
item.description:
The UN's COP31 climate talks were set to spill into overtime Friday as countries remained deadlocked over a draft deal that makes no mention of fossil fuels, with a host of other disputes also snarling negotiations. The talks come with a series of stark reminders of the urgency of climate action, from heatwaves in Europe and devastating floods in Nepal, while a record-breaking El Nino supercharges temperatures. FRANCE 24's Environment Editor Valerie Dekimpe tells us more.

item.description:

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. item.description:
A Rohingya refugee waves Myanmar's national flag as he waits for the arrival of U.N. General Assembly President Khalilur Rahman at a refugee camp in Bangladesh's Cox's Bazar on Nov. 20, 2026. —Salahuddin Ahmed—AFP/Getty Images The world’s top international court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim minority, more than a million of whom remain displaced. The verdict , issued Thursday, is the first time a state has been found responsible for committing genocide in the history of the International Court of Justice, which was established in 1945. In a weekslong military campaign in 2017, Myanmar forces killed at least 10,000 people, including up to 2,109 children under five, and forced more than 700,000 others to flee the country’s northern Rakhine State. item.title: Welcome to Software Beirut
item.description:
Last week, when it briefly looked like the world was collapsing while I sat on the tarmac, I wrote about the arrival of Software Beirut —“where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.” I’m no Tom Friedman , but many people seemed to enjoy the phrase and encouraged me to keep using it even as outages at the FAA, Chase, and Microsoft proved to be isolated incidents unrelated to bad guys using advanced AI. Well, hold my mustache wax! Because I’m doubling down. The fact that all of the software chaos appears to have had boring causes doesn’t negate my point—it improves it. Software Beirut is not an event but an environment, shaped by three forces that arrived at roughly the same time: AI is exposing vulnerabilities in critical software at unprecedented speed; the rush to fix the bugs creates its own hair ball…
